2. Cleaning data¶

In [10]:
ifr_cols = [
    "FLT_DEP_IFR_2",
    "FLT_ARR_IFR_2",
    "FLT_TOT_IFR_2"
]

df[ifr_cols] = df[ifr_cols].fillna(0)

Missing IFR values were previously filled with 0 for general preprocessing purposes. However, this may introduce unrealistic IFR ratios or zero-IFR airports in certain regions.

In [11]:
df["FLT_DATE"] = pd.to_datetime(df["FLT_DATE"], errors="coerce")
In [12]:
df = df.rename(columns={
    "FLT_DEP_1": "departure_flights",
    "FLT_ARR_1": "arrival_flights",
    "FLT_TOT_1": "total_flights",

    "FLT_DEP_IFR_2": "departure_ifr",
    "FLT_ARR_IFR_2": "arrival_ifr",
    "FLT_TOT_IFR_2": "total_ifr",

    "APT_NAME": "airport_name",
    "APT_ICAO": "airport_icao",
    "STATE_NAME": "country"
})

text_fixes = {
    "T\u00c3\u00bcrkiye": "Türkiye",
    "Atat\u00c3\u00bcrk": "Atatürk",
    "G\u00c3\u00b6k\u00c3\u00a7en": "Gökçen",
}

for col in ["airport_name", "country"]:
    for wrong, correct in text_fixes.items():
        df[col] = df[col].str.replace(wrong, correct, regex=False)

df["airport_country"] = (
    df["airport_name"] +
    " (" +
    df["country"] +
    ")"
)

Insight from Sections 3.1-3.2¶

Amsterdam Schiphol Airport recorded the highest total flight activity among all airports in the dataset. However, the Netherlands did not rank as the country with the highest overall flight traffic in Europe.

This suggests that Dutch air traffic is highly concentrated around a single major hub airport. In contrast, countries such as Germany, France, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Türkiye show a more distributed aviation network, where flight activity is spread across multiple major airports rather than dominated by one central hub.

Together, France, Germany, Spain, and the United Kingdom account for nearly half of total European flight activity (48.37%), indicating that major European aviation activity is heavily concentrated in Western Europe.

Network Structure Insight¶

  • The Netherlands relies heavily on one dominant international hub: Amsterdam Schiphol Airport.
  • Germany, France, Spain, and the United Kingdom show broader multi-airport networks, with major traffic distributed across several large airports.
  • This difference helps explain why the busiest airport and the busiest country are not necessarily the same.

Insight from Monthly Flight Patterns¶

The overall European flight trend shows that total air traffic generally peaked in August. However, analysis from the top countries heatmap revealed that many major countries tended to reach their peak activity around July.

This suggests that flight patterns in the largest countries do not always perfectly represent the behavior of Europe as a whole. Seasonal tourism activity from other regions and countries may have contributed to the overall European peak shifting toward August.

Most countries show a consistent seasonal flight pattern, where air traffic gradually increases toward summer and peaks around July–August before declining again near the end of the year.

This recurring pattern appears across multiple European countries, suggesting that flight activity in Europe is strongly influenced by seasonal tourism and summer travel demand.

Tourism-oriented countries such as Greece, Spain, and Portugal show particularly strong increases during peak summer months.

plt.ylabel("Total Flights", fontsize=12)
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.axvspan(
    pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01"),
    pd.Timestamp("2021-12-31"),
    color="red",
    alpha=0.15,
    label="COVID-19 Period"
)

monthly_flights["rolling_mean"] = (
    monthly_flights["total_flights"]
    .rolling(3)
    .mean()
)

plt.plot(
    monthly_flights["FLT_DATE"],
    monthly_flights["rolling_mean"],
    linewidth=3,
    linestyle="--",
    label="3-Month Rolling Mean"
)

min_idx = monthly_flights["total_flights"].idxmin()

min_x = monthly_flights.loc[min_idx, "FLT_DATE"]
min_y = monthly_flights.loc[min_idx, "total_flights"]

plt.annotate(
    "COVID Collapse",
    xy=(min_x, min_y),
    xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2019-01-01"), 1000000),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2)
)

import matplotlib.dates as mdates

plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(
    mdates.YearLocator()
)

plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_formatter(
    mdates.DateFormatter('%Y')
)

plt.legend()

plt.tight_layout()

filepath = os.path.join("plots", "monthly_flights_over_time.png")
plt.savefig(filepath, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
plt.show()

European flight activity showed a clear seasonal pattern before COVID-19. From 2016–2019, flights consistently increased toward mid-year and usually peaked around July before declining toward the end of the year.

A major disruption occurred in early 2020 when COVID-19 caused a dramatic collapse in air traffic across Europe. After the pandemic, flight patterns became more unstable and less predictable compared to the relatively consistent pre-pandemic cycles.

The 3-month rolling mean also confirms both the repeating seasonal trend before COVID-19 and the significant disruption caused by the pandemic.

Insight from Sections 3.8–3.9¶

From 2016 to 2019, European flight activity showed a strong seasonal pattern, where air traffic generally increased from the beginning of the year toward mid-year before gradually declining again near the end of the year.

The overall European flight trend indicates that total air traffic typically peaked around August. However, analysis from several major countries showed that many of them individually tended to peak around July. This suggests that flight behavior in the largest countries does not always perfectly represent the overall European pattern.

Several unusual situations also appeared in later years:

  • 2020 recorded its peak activity in January, not because of a seasonal shift, but because it was the last normal period before the COVID-19 pandemic caused a dramatic collapse in European air traffic.

  • 2021 showed a different recovery pattern, where peak activity occurred in August, likely influenced by delayed travel recovery and changing restrictions during the pandemic period.

  • 2022 recorded its peak in May, but the dataset only contains data up to May 2022, so this should not be interpreted as a complete yearly seasonal pattern.

Overall, the dataset reveals a clear seasonal cycle in European flights while also highlighting how extraordinary events such as COVID-19 temporarily disrupted normal aviation behavior.

Handling Missing IFR Values¶

The IFR-related columns contained a large number of missing values. Instead of removing rows with missing IFR data, the missing values were filled with 0.

This decision was made to preserve overall airport activity across different time periods. Removing rows with missing IFR values would exclude airports that may only lack IFR reporting temporarily in certain months, even though they have valid IFR activity in other periods.

For example, major airports in countries such as France, Germany, and Spain also contained missing IFR records in some observations. Dropping these rows entirely could bias the analysis by underrepresenting total airport operations.

Therefore, missing IFR values were treated as 0 under the assumption that no IFR activity was recorded for those specific observations.

Some airports exceeded 100% IFR percentage, indicating possible inconsistencies in the source dataset or differences in reporting methodology.

4. Key Findings¶

  • Amsterdam Schiphol was the busiest individual airport in the dataset, but the Netherlands was not the busiest country overall. This indicates that Dutch flight activity is highly concentrated in one major hub.
  • France, Germany, Spain, and the United Kingdom contributed nearly half of total European flight activity, showing that air traffic was strongly concentrated in Western Europe.
  • European flights followed a clear seasonal pattern before COVID-19, generally increasing toward summer and declining near the end of the year.
  • COVID-19 caused a major disruption in 2020, breaking the stable seasonal pattern seen from 2016 to 2019.
  • Several major airports recovered after the initial pandemic shock, but the recovery pattern was less stable than the pre-pandemic cycle.
  • Istanbul Ataturk showed a distinct structural drop after 2019 because passenger operations shifted to IGA Istanbul Airport, making it a separate event from the COVID-19 decline.
  • IFR percentage results should be interpreted carefully because some airports exceeded 100%, indicating possible reporting differences or source-data inconsistencies.

5. Limitations¶

  • Missing IFR values were filled with 0 to preserve airport activity records, but this can bias IFR percentage calculations downward for airports with incomplete IFR reporting.
  • The dataset ends in May 2022, so 2022 should not be interpreted as a complete year when comparing annual or seasonal patterns.
  • IFR percentages above 100% suggest that IFR-related columns may follow a different reporting methodology from total flight columns, or that the source data contains inconsistencies.
  • This analysis focuses on descriptive EDA. It does not model causality or forecast future traffic.

6. Recommended Next Steps¶

  • Compare IFR results using alternative missing-value strategies, such as leaving missing values as NaN or excluding airports with incomplete IFR records.
  • Add airport-level recovery metrics, such as percentage decline from 2019 to 2020 and recovery rate from 2020 to 2022.
  • Separate full-year comparisons from partial-year comparisons to avoid over-interpreting 2022.
